1.pericope_label: Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit.

schools.summary: Ellicott compares the traveller's eager search for the early fig to the prophet's search for a good man and finds the psalmist's experience, that the godly man ceases; Keil and Delitzsch set out the whole chapter in order as a penitential prayer rising through belief in God's fidelity to hope, then to petition, answer and praise.

Gill takes the complaint in the prophet's own name or in the name of the church of his time; Calvin rejects the reading that makes the lament concern punishment rather than wickedness, refuses a rendering he thinks too free, and takes the land as personified and stripped of all its fruit rather than left with a few gleanings.

Clarke reads the prophet as the last man standing, a solitary grape escaped from the general gathering, and reports that the word may be rendered late figs as against the early ripe fig of superior quality; Wesley makes the land itself the complainant, once well stored and now having few good in it.

Henry weighs the date of the description, reporting that some take it as a prediction of a later reign since it scarcely suits the one named, and preferring an earlier reign or the beginning of the reforming one, since even at its best much remained amiss.

debates.question: Does the lament concern punishment or wickedness?

positions.position: Wickedness: the following verse makes it plain, though some refer it to punishment already inflicted.
The decay of piety and the growth of ungodliness, the good man being as rare as the early fig late in the season.

debates.question: Under which reign was this spoken?

positions.position: Some take it as a prediction of a later and worse reign, since it scarcely suits the one named; better an earlier reign, or the beginning of the reforming one before its reformation took effect.

outliers.claim: Rejects the rendering that makes the prophet a man seeking summer fruit and burning with disappointed desire as too free and impossible to get out of the words, and prefers the emptier picture of a land stripped after harvest to the reading that leaves a few gleanings standing for a few just men.

themes: Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit.

2.pericope_label: The good man is perished out of the earth: and there is none upright among men: they all lie in wait for blood; they hunt every man his brother with a net.

schools.summary: Ellicott derives the word for net from a verb meaning to shut up and notes that such a net served fisherman and fowler alike, so that men lay wait for one another as hunters for wild beasts; Keil and Delitzsch render the complaint as the universal corruption which the church confesses in its prayer.

Gill defines the good man as one who has received the grace of God and is particularly merciful to those in distress, and is careful that the perishing means bodily death and not the perishing of graces or souls; Calvin gives the philology of the same term and of its companion, takes the clauses for a thirst after blood and for perfidy, and observes that the land is made to accuse its own children.

Clarke expounds the hunting with a net as an allusion to the ancient duel between the net-man and the pursuer, and notes that a translator who missed the allusion rendered the clause that they hunt every man his brother for his destruction.

debates.question: What is the hunting with a net?

positions.position: An allusion to the ancient duel in which one combatant cast a net over his opponent while the other pursued him when the cast missed.
The ordinary net of fisherman or fowler: men lay wait for one another as hunters for wild beasts.
A figure of perfidy, the preceding clause being a thirst after blood.

debates.question: In what sense has the good man perished?

positions.position: By bodily death, not by the perishing of his graces or his comforts or his soul.
By the universal corruption which the church confesses.

outliers.claim: Observes that the manner adopted here is more emphatic than if God had pronounced the words in his own name, since the land is introduced accusing its own children, confessing its guilt, and anticipating God's judgment by acknowledging itself contaminated by its own inhabitants.

themes: The good man is perished out of the earth: and there is none upright among men: they all lie in wait for blood; they hunt every man his brother with a net.

3.pericope_label: That they may do evil with both hands earnestly, the prince asketh, and the judge asketh for a reward; and the great man, he uttereth his mischievous desire: so they wrap it up. The best of them is as a brier: the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge: the day of thy watchmen and thy visitation cometh; now shall be their perplexity. Trust ye not in a friend, put ye not confidence in a guide: keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom. For the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.

schools.summary: Ellicott reports a modern Jewish translation made under a chief rabbi's supervision which sidesteps the oxymoron of doing evil well, renders the closing clause as twisting and perverting justice, and glosses the day of the watchmen as the time the prophets had foreseen; Keil and Delitzsch render the best man as a thorn-bush which only pricks and injures.

Gill takes the adverb as strenuously and reports the readings of the versions, says the briers are good for nothing but burning, and fences the warning against trusting a friend so that it does not lessen the value of friendship but shows how far the age had degenerated; Calvin reads the same verses as iniquity arrived at its highest point, faithfulness and humanity both gone.

Clarke traces the venality of prince and judge into his own country's history before the great charter, notices the thick thorn hedges of that country, and reprints a personal note written a quarter of a century before about friends who had deceived him; Wesley identifies the great man at court and calls the coming day surely and unavoidably at hand.

debates.question: How is the phrase about doing evil well to be taken?

positions.position: As strenuously and diligently, the wicked being more industrious in evil than good men in good.
A modern rendering avoids the oxymoron by making it concern the evil which their hands should amend, which harmonises with the rest of the passage.

debates.question: What is the force of the comparison to briers?

positions.position: They are useless in themselves and cannot be touched without wounding whoever comes near, the allusion being to the thick thorn hedges of the country.
They only prick and injure.
They are good for nothing but burning.

outliers.claim: Reprints a note he had written on the warning against trusting a friend a quarter of a century earlier — that several whom he delighted to call friends had deceived him, that had he followed certain guides he should have gone to perdition, and that his wife alone never deceived him — adding that after twenty-seven years he finds no cause to alter it.

themes: That they may do evil with both hands earnestly, the prince asketh, and the judge asketh for a reward; and the great man, he uttereth his mischievous desire: so they wrap it up.
The best of them is as a brier: the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge: the day of thy watchmen and thy visitation cometh; now shall be their perplexity.
Trust ye not in a friend, put ye not confidence in a guide: keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom.
For the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.

7.pericope_label: Therefore I will look unto the Lord; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me. Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light unto me.

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the turn its landscape, the eyes lifted to the everlasting hills because of the gloom settled on the earth, and makes the grammatical point that the word for enemy is strictly a female enemy used collectively, proposing two cities named together in a psalm of exile; Keil and Delitzsch mark the church rising through belief in God's fidelity to confident hope.

Gill expands the looking into an inventory of prayer and confidence and expectation and reports the Targum's reference to the Word of the Lord, and extends the enemy from the literal invaders to the great enemy of mankind and to the men of the world who watch for the halting of the saints; Calvin reads the verse as the church repelling the temptation of mockery, sharper to noble minds than death.

Clarke states the principle that to rejoice over the fall of any man betrays a malignant spirit and illustrates it from religious controversy in his own day; Wesley reads the looking as the act of one set in a watchtower observing all that stirs.

Henry draws the rule that the less reason we have to delight in any creature the more reason we have to delight in God, and keeps the indignation within the covenant relation, just because sin provoked it.

debates.question: Who is the enemy addressed?

positions.position: The Assyrians and Chaldeans, the fall being the idolatry and captivity and the rising the restoration.
A female enemy used collectively, probably two named cities whose fall was to be final.
The literal invaders, and also the great enemy of mankind and the men of the world who rejoice at the falls of the saints.

debates.question: Why does the prophet turn to the Lord at this point?

positions.position: Because no confidence can be put in friends on earth: the less reason to delight in any creature, the more to delight in God.
Because of the gloom settled on the earth, so that he lifts his eyes to the hills on which the light of God's presence rests.

outliers.claim: Illustrates the malignity of rejoicing over another's fall from religious controversy in his own day, where opponents holding what he calls an impure creed exulted publicly over the fall of men holding a purer one, and judges that in God's sight the exultation may have been worse than the fall exulted in.

themes: Therefore I will look unto the Lord; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me.
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light unto me.

9.pericope_label: I will bear the indignation of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he plead my cause, and execute judgment for me: he will bring me forth to the light, and I shall behold his righteousness. Then she that is mine enemy shall see it, and shame shall cover her which said unto me, Where is the Lord thy God? mine eyes shall behold her: now shall she be trodden down as the mire of the streets.

schools.summary: Ellicott instances the king who chose to fall into the hand of the Lord rather than of man and says this is the temper of all penitents under chastisement, and reads the enemy's treading down as the answer to the taunt that Israel's God was powerless; Keil and Delitzsch mark the church looking for the Lord to procure it justice and humble the foe.

Gill notes the Targum's preface and reports that some Jewish authorities read the enemy as Rome, turning the identification round upon papal Rome; Calvin analyses the two supports by which the church sustains patience, distinguishes confession from repentance by two who owned their sin without repenting, and notices that the enemies are figured as an envious woman.

Clarke identifies the speakers as the penitent captives and warns the slanderers that woe is theirs when God pleads for the fallen who have returned, and reports the ruin of the enemy city with bricks from its rubbish lying before him as he writes; Wesley glosses the pleading and the righteousness of the promised salvation.

debates.question: Who is the enemy that shall see and be trodden down?

positions.position: Babylon, whose sun-dried brick walls dissolved until no vestige of the city remained.
The enemy who taunted the Jews with the powerlessness of their God.
Some Jewish authorities read Rome, meaning the Christians; but it would not be amiss to understand papal Rome against the church of God.

debates.question: What makes the bearing of the indignation genuine repentance?

positions.position: Two supports: the sins set before her so that she humbles herself before a just judge, and the hope of forgiveness from which confidence of deliverance arises.
The temper of all penitents under chastisement, choosing to fall into the hand of the Lord rather than of man.

outliers.claim: Distinguishes confession from repentance by two examples of men who owned that they had sinned without repenting at all, one confessing freely and the other only under compulsion, and concludes that whoever clamours against God or murmurs has not yet been made sensible of his sins.

themes: I will bear the indignation of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he plead my cause, and execute judgment for me: he will bring me forth to the light, and I shall behold his righteousness.

Then she that is mine enemy shall see it, and shame shall cover her which said unto me, Where is the Lord thy God? mine eyes shall behold her: now shall she be trodden down as the mire of the streets.

11.pericope_label: In the day that thy walls are to be built, in that day shall the decree be far removed. In that day also he shall come even to thee from Assyria, and from the fortified cities, and from the fortress even to the river, and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain. Notwithstanding the land shall be desolate because of them that dwell therein, for the fruit of their doings.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the decree as an appointed statute and prefers the interpretation that it concerned distant nations pressing into the kingdom, translates the gathering impersonally as coming from all parts of the earth, and discerns on the horizon of the vision the assembly of the nations at Pentecost; Keil and Delitzsch supply the verses plainly.

Gill twice rejects the reading that makes these verses an address to the enemy, takes them as a continued address to the church, and distributes the desolation over three visitations while explaining why the warning stands where it does; Calvin admits obscurity in the words and reports the proposal that one is a proper name.

Clarke cannot think the verse threatens Jerusalem rather than promising, sets two translations of the gathering side by side and prefers the one that gives an easy sense, and removes the difficulty of the desolation by rendering the verb as past; Wesley identifies the decree as the royal order forbidding the rebuilding and measures the interval before the promises took effect.

debates.question: What is the decree that shall be far removed?

positions.position: The royal order that forbade the rebuilding, now abolished.
An appointed statute: either the law of separation between Jew and Gentile, or a decree concerning distant nations who should press into the kingdom.
God's purpose to deliver the people into captivity, now to be far removed.

debates.question: How is the desolation to be reconciled with the promise?

positions.position: By the tense: the verb should be rendered as past, the land having been desolate during the captivity.
It is future, and stands here partly to prevent wicked men promising themselves impunity and partly to prevent good men despairing.
It is bitterness still in the cup, the near desolation rising amid triumphant expectation.
The promises simply did not take effect for more than two hundred years.

outliers.claim: Prefers a translation of the gathering that runs from Assyria to Egypt and thence to the Euphrates and from sea to sea and mountain to mountain, on the ground that the rival rendering leaves nobody able to say where the fortified cities spoken of are to be found.

themes: In the day that thy walls are to be built, in that day shall the decree be far removed.
In that day also he shall come even to thee from Assyria, and from the fortified cities, and from the fortress even to the river, and from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain.
Notwithstanding the land shall be desolate because of them that dwell therein, for the fruit of their doings.

14.pericope_label: Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage, which dwell solitarily in the wood, in the midst of Carmel: let them feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old. According to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt will I shew unto him marvellous things.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the rod as a shepherd's crook and describes the flock as dwelling alone among idolaters or apart from other nations after the return, and cites a contemporary book on the eastern pasture lands which had lately brought their fertility into prominence; Keil and Delitzsch mark the prayer for renewed manifestations of grace answered by the promise to renew the wonders of old.

Gill lays out three possible speakers for the prayer and prefers the prophet's own, and states the answer as a deliverance as great as the bringing out of Egypt; Calvin argues that the passage has more force because entreaty was interposed first, and sharpens the relation between prayer and answer, God promising to outdo their hopes.

Clarke insists that the word most certainly means the shepherd's crook and that no rod of correction is intended, and calls the named places proverbially fruitful in pasturage; Wesley notes the allusion to shepherds guiding sheep with a staff and reads the wood as the solitary and endangered state of the captives.

Henry draws the rule that when God is about to deliver his people he stirs up their friends to pray, calls this a prophetic prayer amounting to a promise, and develops the flock in the forest into an allegory of the exile.

debates.question: Whose prayer is the request to feed the flock?

positions.position: Possibly the Father's to the Son, or the Son's to his ministers, but most likely the prophet's own to God.
The prophet's own prayer for his people, amounting to a promise of what is asked.
Christ directing his officers.

debates.question: What is the rod?

positions.position: Most certainly the shepherd's crook; no rod of correction or affliction is intended, nor does the word mean such.
A shepherd's crook, the people being led as a flock.

outliers.claim: Sharpens the relation between the prayer and its answer: the prophet asked only that God would feed his people and do kind things for them, and God replies that he will show them marvellous things and outdo their hopes and expectations, so that the deliverance is to be a work of wonder and of grace.

themes: Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage, which dwell solitarily in the wood, in the midst of Carmel: let them feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old.
According to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt will I shew unto him marvellous things.

16.pericope_label: The nations shall see and be confounded at all their might: they shall lay their hand upon their mouth, their ears shall be deaf. They shall lick the dust like a serpent, they shall move out of their holes like worms of the earth: they shall be afraid of the Lord our God, and shall fear because of thee.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in the licking of the dust the doom pronounced on the serpent and applies it to the determined enemies of the Lord and his people.

Gill takes the nations first as the Babylonians ashamed of their boasted power and then extends the verse to the confusion of the Gentile world at the spread of the gospel, and gives both a natural and a ceremonial explanation of the licking of the dust; Calvin makes the verse an answer to a particular anxiety, glosses the hand on the mouth as meaning they shall not dare to boast, keeps the licking simple as lying prostrate, and derives the word for their holes from a root meaning to close up.

Clarke declines to choose among the historical applications and says the verses may be understood as ultimately applying to a final restoration under the gospel; Wesley combines the two senses of the licking as a submissive and servile subjection and renders the holes as strongholds and fastnesses.

debates.question: What does the licking of the dust picture?

positions.position: The manner of the eastern nations in complimenting kings, bowing so low as to take the dust into their mouths.
Nothing else but lying prostrate on the earth, low and creeping like serpents.
The doom pronounced on the serpent, applied to the enemies of the Lord.
A submissive and servile testimony of subjection.

debates.question: What are the holes they move out of?

positions.position: Lurking-places, since the prophet is speaking of worms, though elsewhere the same word is applied to citadels.
Their strongholds and fastnesses.

outliers.claim: Declines to choose among the historical applications, holding that whether the verses be referred to the return from captivity or to the later prosperity under the Maccabees, they may be understood as ultimately applying to a final restoration under the gospel.

themes: The nations shall see and be confounded at all their might: they shall lay their hand upon their mouth, their ears shall be deaf.
They shall lick the dust like a serpent, they shall move out of their holes like worms of the earth: they shall be afraid of the Lord our God, and shall fear because of thee.

18.pericope_label: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy. He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that the prophet concludes with an allusion to the meaning of his own name and claims that the gracious character ascribed to God here is unparalleled in the Bible among human utterances, being his response to the words God spoke of himself to Moses; Keil and Delitzsch supply the closing verses plainly.

Gill denies that there is any god besides and insists that the anger is a displeasure at sin rather than at the persons of his people, so that properly it is not in God at all but rather in appearance than reality; Calvin turns the comparison into an argument, answers the objection that every nation thought its gods ready to pardon, and prescribes the application by which each of the faithful must conclude that God will be merciful to him.

Clarke reads the opening as a challenge to idol-worshippers and enumerates five characters in answer to it, and records that five manuscripts and four ancient versions read our sins rather than their sins.

debates.question: On what ground is God said to be without a like?

positions.position: On his pardoning grace, there being no god besides him and none so great in the perfections of his nature.

Not that he forgives, which every nation claimed of its gods, but that having received the children of Abraham into favour he kept his covenant inviolably though their sins a thousand times stood in the way.
On five characters answering a challenge to idol-worshippers to show his like.
On a gracious character unparalleled in the Bible among human utterances.

debates.question: In what sense does God turn again?

positions.position: Not by any change in himself: the anger is a displeasure at sin, rather in appearance than in reality, and he returns when they are brought to a sense of sin.
By pitying their state and subduing their iniquities and casting their sins into the depths.

outliers.claim: Calls the application the true logic of religion: it avails little to understand something in general about God's mercy or to preach free remission at large, unless each of the faithful concludes that since God forgives because he is by nature inclined to mercy, he will therefore be merciful to us; without that conclusion all we have heard of God's goodness vanishes away.

themes: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

20.pericope_label: Thou wilt perform the truth to Jacob, and the mercy to Abraham, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the closing words are gloriously taken up some centuries afterwards in the song of the priest who spoke of God performing the mercy promised to the fathers and remembering his covenant; Keil and Delitzsch give the verse without comment, having marked the close as the prophet's praise of the mercy of the Lord.

Gill takes the promise as faithfully performed to the patriarch's posterity, natural and spiritual, and especially to Israelites indeed; Calvin makes the verse the ground of the whole hymn, that the faithful do not learn by their own understanding what God is but embrace the mercy he offers in his word, and notes that of the two terms characterising the covenant the mercy comes first in order of cause.

Clarke identifies the later song as a quotation of this prophecy fulfilled in the incarnation, quotes the Chaldee paraphrase at length for its spirit and propriety, explains the phrase about the divisions, and closes with a direct address to his reader.

debates.question: What is the relation of this verse to what precedes?

positions.position: It is the ground of the whole: without God's word we can form no idea of his grace but an uncertain one, so the faithful receive what he has testified.
It is the promise made to the patriarch, faithfully performed to his posterity.
It is the close taken up centuries later in a song about the mercy promised to the fathers.

debates.question: Which of truth and mercy comes first?

positions.position: The mercy, in order of cause, since God is not induced to it by anything outside himself.

outliers.claim: Quotes the Chaldee paraphrase of the closing verse at length for its spirit and propriety, explaining that its phrase about the divisions refers to the covenant made when the pieces were divided, and ends the chapter by turning from the text to address his reader directly.

themes: Thou wilt perform the truth to Jacob, and the mercy to Abraham, which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old.
